name: The Chabuca Granda Cedar

location.address: Avenida 28 de Julio, block 6, Miraflores, in front of the singer Chabuca Granda's former house

access: Free, standing on the public pavement of Avenida 28 de Julio
transport: Central Miraflores, walkable from Parque Kennedy
verify_notes: Registro 001-2020-MM, Miraflores' first (and so far only) heritage tree, declared by Ordenanza N. 555-2020/MM on 28 Oct 2020 (sinia.minam.gob.pe confirms ordinance existence but the fetched copy returned a different district's cedro by mistake, so ordinance text itself not directly read; municipality's own page + infobae both independently confirm the story and location). The story: on 3 September 1977 (her own birthday), singer-songwriter Chabuca Granda physically embraced this cedar to stop municipal workers felling it outside her house on Av 28 de Julio cuadra 6. She later wrote the poem 'Cancion al arbol del canto' about it. No age, height or girth published in any source found; do not invent one, leave age_estimate empty and let the page ask the reader. Species: Cedrela odorata is the tropical/Spanish cedar native to Peru, commonly called 'cedro'; matches Wikidata Q137303616. Wikidata coordinate (-12.127867, -77.027134) sits on Av 28 de Julio in Miraflores, consistent with the cuadra-6 address, so marked confirmed rather than approximate. Recognition criteria per ordinance: development stage, height, diameter, vulnerable-species status, cultural significance. Still referenced as current in a Jan 2026 infobae roundup of Lima's 26 heritage trees, so the register entry is not stale.

name: The Olive of San Martin de Porres

location.address: Bosque El Olivar, Calle Hermilio Hernandez (block 1), next to Casa Museo Marina Nunez del Prado, near Calle Antero Aspillaga 291, San Isidro

access: Free, inside Bosque El Olivar, a public park open daily
transport: San Isidro, walkable within the park district; several bus routes serve Av Los Incas
verify_notes: Registro 003-2020-MSI, declared by Ordenanza N. 535-MSI (published El Peruano, 21 Feb 2021). Called locally the 'Olivo de San Martin de Porres': specialised studies cited by a 21 May 2026 official San Isidro municipal press release (gob.pe) say it was likely planted between 1637 and 1643 by Fray Martin de Porres (the Peruvian Dominican saint), making it close to 400 years old; infobae's Jan 2026 roundup independently gives 'over 380 years', calling it the longest-lived of Lima's 26 heritage trees. Two sources agree closely so age band set 380-400 rather than picking one figure. The same May 2026 release says SERFOR (national forestry service) formally recognised San Isidro for conserving this tree as part of Peru's new national heritage-tree register, which is also strong evidence the tree is alive and cared for as of a few months ago. Stands in Bosque El Olivar, Lima's old colonial olive grove (over 1,600 trees, planted from stock brought from Spain in the 1500s-1600s), immediately beside Casa Museo Marina Nunez del Prado; that context (an olive grove) makes a bridge claim tempting, i.e. that this specific tree dates from the grove's founding, but only THIS tree's own designation and the cited planting-date study are used here, not the grove's general age. Lima's near-total desert climate (rain effectively never) is the striking fact for the writer: this tree has survived four centuries on irrigation and fog alone, not rainfall. No girth/diameter published in any source found.

name: San Martin's Ombu

location.address: Parque El Carmen (Quinta de los Libertadores), Pueblo Libre

access: Free, in Parque El Carmen, a public park
transport: Central Pueblo Libre, walkable from Plaza Bolivar
verify_notes: Registro 1, declared Cultural and Historical Heritage of Pueblo Libre by Ordenanza 570-MPL in 2020 (busquedas.elperuano.pe / El Peruano confirms the ordinance exists, matches Wikidata Q137303617). Local tradition, repeated by multiple outlets (infobae, andina.pe, El Comercio, Peru21, Latina), says General Jose de San Martin himself planted it in 1821 during his stay at the Quinta de los Libertadores, having brought the ombu seed from Argentina, shortly before independence and before handing the campaign to Simon Bolivar. Infobae itself hedges with 'according to legend' for the personal-planting detail, so verify_notes flags that the PLANTING DATE (1821, i.e. now ~205 years) is well corroborated but the claim that SAN MARTIN HIMSELF did the planting rather than someone in his household is legend-level, not documentary; the writer should keep that distinction rather than stating it as flat fact. Height reported as 'more than 25 metres' (infobae 2022) vs 'more than 30 metres' (elcomercio via search summary), so treat height as roughly 25-30m and do not pick one figure. The park underwent a lighting/fencing/pergola renovation around the tree (2022), which is independent evidence the tree was alive and being actively cared for then; no more recent confirmation found in this pass, so curation_status flagged rather than fully clean. No girth published. This is the single most famous tree of the fourteen candidates and the strongest anchor for a Lima page: a specific national hero's own planting, in a public park, with a real story.

name: The Ceiba of Parque Ernesto Alayza Grundy

location.address: Green area of Pasaje 65 NN, at the entrance to Parque Ernesto Alayza Grundy, Calle Victor Maurtua (block 1), San Isidro

access: Free, in the entrance green area of a public park
transport: San Isidro, walkable within the district
verify_notes: Registro 002-2020-MSI, declared by Ordenanza N. 535-MSI alongside the Araucaria and Olive (published El Peruano, 21 Feb 2021), matches Wikidata Q137303619. Confirmed still standing and included as a stop on San Isidro's newly launched 'Ruta de los Arboles Patrimoniales' (municipality + SERFOR, opened 27 June 2026), which describes San Isidro's ceibo specimens as uncommon for the species in this urban zone; that same route article names two ceibo trees in the district (this one and another on Calle Alfredo Roldan Seminario), so double check before writing that this is the district's only one. No age, height or girth published in any source found; leave age_estimate empty and let the page ask the reader. Kapok trees are native to tropical lowland forest, not Lima's coastal desert, so how this specimen is irrigated/thrives here could be worth a line for the writer if a further source turns up; not confirmed in this pass.

name: The Araucaria of El Olivar

location.address: Bosque El Olivar, at the corner of Calle 24 de Abril (block 2) and Calle Las Amazonas (block 1), San Isidro

access: Free, inside Bosque El Olivar, a public park open daily
transport: San Isidro, walkable within the park district
verify_notes: Registro 001-2020-MSI, declared by Ordenanza N. 535-MSI (El Peruano, 21 Feb 2021), matches Wikidata Q137303618. A 21 May 2026 official San Isidro press release gives roughly 80 years old and about 44 metres tall, called 'one of the tallest and most majestic trees in Lima'; a 27 June 2026 infobae piece on the district's new heritage-tree route gives 41 metres. Height set as roughly 41-44m rather than a single figure since two close but non-identical official-adjacent figures exist; age kept at a broad 70-90 year band around the stated ~80 years since no planting record was cited, only an estimate. Species is Araucaria columnaris (Cook Pine / New Caledonia pine), not the more common Araucaria araucana (monkey puzzle) or Araucaria heterophylla (Norfolk Island pine) already used elsewhere on the site; matched to the existing site convention 'Cook Pine (Araucaria columnaris)'. Stands inside the same olive grove as the San Martin de Porres olive (lim_002), a short walk away, so these two plus the Ceiba (lim_004) form a real cluster within San Isidro.
